pr_title: [PoC] lib: os: fdtable: Add syscalls for POSIX read/write/close/ioctl operations
pr_body:
Fdtable is a kernel-level structure, so functions accessing it, like
read(), write(), close(), should be syscalls. This conversion however
emphasizes a difference between "syscall" and "C standard library
function". C stdlib functions should be represented by just a
standard linkage symbol, and can be used even without prototype.
Syscall is however a special code sequence, which may require special
attributes and thus a prototype for usage. To deal with these
distinction, we define a convention that "sys_name" is a syscall,
while "name" is a normal C function (implemented as a wrapper around
syscall). (And we also need to define "_name" to interface with Newlib
(actually, just "_write".))

Fixes: #25407

Signed-off-by: Paul Sokolovsky <paul.sokolovsky@linaro.org>
pr_comments: Ok, read/write/close syscall are now clean re: build. Will proceed with ioctl tomorrow, then test is the next step after that.

> Getting "undefined reference to _write" and "undefined reference to _read" in libc_nano.a . It doesn't jump out at me immediately why that might be the case.

For the record, to elaborate what happened there. Prebuilt Newlib, as shipped with Zephyr SDK is call into write to dump some error on stdout/stderr. The issue is that the actual function called is inconsistent among the builds for different architectures. For example, x86 calls write(), while ARM - _write(). My original idea was to make _write() a syscall, while write() a normal userspace func, that due to the above, I fell back to Linux-like convention of sys_write() being a syscall, and write()/_write() userspace funcs.

Thinking about it, ARM newlib build is right here, while x86 is wrong. The whole idea of underscore-prefixed functions is that they don't provide full POSIX semantics. So, if x86 called _write, we wouldn't need to define write() for !CONFIG_POSIX_API case, and @cfriedt would never get confused by calling write() on a socket in this case, and getting output dumped to console. Actually, that would be the right way to resolve the issue, so let me even try to submit https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/sdk-ng/issues/221 (though I'm not sure who would be looking into that).
In the meantime, pushed a commit with ioctl() conversion to syscall.

> In the meantime, pushed a commit with ioctl() conversion to syscall.

And it's the usual suspect, @andrewboie, I'm sure there's nothing new in this [#if 0](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/25443/files#diff-09297f7c837caac9222160d791c83a8cR286), it was expected all along (and again, why it spent so much time in backlog).

**All checks passed.**

@andrewboie:

> By the way the other syscalls look fine, I'd suggest splitting out ioctl into another PR as I see no impediments to getting the others in, and ioctl may take some time.

That was the plan. But another part of plan was to add read()/write() tests to an existing socket test. However, it happens that existing test calls fcntl() in one of testcases, which is implemented in terms of ioctl(). So, I would need to work that around by introducing separate adhoc test just for socket read()/write(). And fairly speaking, I already worked around that pretty well by not writing tests :-I. That would be just continuation of that approach - forge a test which kinda shows that something works, while it actually won't work for end users (fcntl, etc.).

Besides, if it's not done now, I don't know for how long it won't be done again, with all painful recalling that "you can't pass va_list across system calls", etc. So, I decided to proceed further with this.

This time I however decided to make sure I read up https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/reference/usermode/index.html section. And I find some descriptions not detailed enough, and have some questions to clarify (in other comment threads).

@andrewboie:

Ok, I'm going to push further commits and/or rebase, which may make inline comments threads less accessible, so reposting questions mentioned above here at the top level (originally at https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/25443#discussion_r430663339)

> That implies that the kernel would then walk arbitrary stack data that the user provided.

Well, I wouldn't call it "walk the stack", just "access a few words on stack". The biggest risk I see is that va_list doesn't really have to refer to stack, but can be crafted to point to arbitrary memory.

But let's assume it's legitimate reference to stack. Please help me to understand what bad things happen if we don't Z_SYSCALL_MEMORY_READ() this reference in a syscall verify handler. Let's consider that a user stack has just 2 words left and will underflow afterwards, but kernel syscall will want to access 3 words.

I tried to find answer in the docs, and don't see detailed enough description. Actually, some details confusing. I traced Z_SYSCALL_MEMORY_READ to https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/guides/porting/arch.html?highlight=arch_buffer_validate#_CPPv420arch_buffer_validatePv6size_ti , 

> Given a memory region, return whether the **current memory management hardware configuration** would allow a user thread to read/write that region.

(Emphasis mine.) Reading such a description, I picture following 2-stage syscall handling sequence:

1. Syscall transfer to kernel mode, but MPU mapping still remains userspace. That's how verify handler is called.
2. A trivial implementation of arch_buffer_validate() thus would just try to read/write each byte in a provided buffer. This would be inefficient, but correct implementation.
3. Only after that, MPU mapping is changed. And possibly changed drastically, like flat mapping is installed, allowing kernel to access entire CPU address space. A more natural solution would be to just enable an MPU region for kernel memory. But then userspace map would still be installed, and then explicit Z_SYSCALL_MEMORY_READ step isn't strictly required.

Is this something resembling reality? It's hard to believe in that, given that verify handler is what calls implementation handler, and there's nothing in there which looks like switching memory map. But then, why arch_buffer_validate() doc refers to "current memory management **hardware** configuration". Hardware configuration by that time can be quite different. And arch_buffer_validate() potentially could be implemented just as series of bounds checks against memory domains configured for calling threads, which has nothing to do with "current hardware configuration" (which could a flat all-addressspace map, again).

 Summing up IMHO there're following issues with https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/reference/usermode/syscalls.html :

1. It doesn't specify at which point userspace memory map is switched to kernel-space memory map, which is IMHO important point.
2. It doesn't specify possible examples of what kernel-space memory map have. I understand this is inherently platform-specific, but the talk is exactly about giving a few possible rights, to set *bounds* of expectations right. E.g. can it be full address space enabled for read-write? If yes, say so. Can it be just a userspace map, with a single extra memory region for kernel r/w data enabled? If yes, say so. Note that "full address space" case effectively means that Zephyr userspace support can work with just a single MPU region (for thread stack, + background region to make the rest R/O), and then kernel space map is just disabling MPU - I never read about such frugal requirements).
3. The references to "current hardware configuration" in arch_buffer_validate() are confusing and may not correspond to reality (and thus should be removed).

Thanks for clarifications.

`arch_buffer_validate()` (which is the function these memory validation macros are built on) regardless of what the underlying hardware is (MPU, MMU with identity tables, MMU with virtual memory) checks whether the buffer being passed in is accessible to the user thread that made the system call.

That's it. That's all it does.

Your conception on how the underlying hardware is working, some notion of a massive memory map switch, is not actually true. And the underlying HW implementation is irrelevant anyway. I don't know why you are going off on this tangent. Assume that these verify macros correctly note whether the user thread has access to the provided buffer and leave it there.

> But let's assume it's legitimate reference to stack. Please help me to understand what bad things happen if we don't Z_SYSCALL_MEMORY_READ() this reference in a syscall verify handler.

How can you possibly "assume" that its a legitimate stack reference? You have to prove all of this. You can't "assume" anything in a system call verifier, other than that anything passed in from user mode could potentially be malicious. What if it's actually a malicious area of memory that looks like a va_list but is actually crafted to get the kernel to reveal sensitive information? The possibilities are endless, use your imagination.

We are not passing va_lists through system calls. You will never find an operating system that does that. Drop it.

> arch_buffer_validate() (which is the function these memory validation macros are built on) regardless of what the underlying hardware is (MPU, MMU with identity tables, MMU with virtual memory) checks whether the buffer being passed in is accessible to the user thread that made the system call.

Then its description is not exactly correct and thus confusing (and needs fixing). Please ack whether this is true, and I'll prepare a patch (unless you want to fix it yourself).

> I don't know why you are going off on this tangent.

Because "to understand how to use it, I need to understand how it works". I'm surprised you'd expect anything else from a colleague of trade. And I address to you, as the main author of that facility, to help me understand some aspects of it.

> Assume that these verify macros correctly ...

I like your attitude (every programmer should have it), but let's for a moment imagine that not everything is perfect in your realm. I don't try to judge the code, given that I myself learn the stuff, but as a learner, I point out a few issues with the docs - some details are missing, some vice versa seem to provide details which are confusing if not incorrect. There're actually more like small typo-thinkos, and functions mentioned are not cross-linked in the rendered docs (they're in .rst). I'd like to take a chance to improve at least something there as I look thru it.

You might not notice, but I pushed a new commit which does exactly that. I intend to ping you when the build is green (it's not so far). I think you should consider an approach where ioctl() is not a system call, but a function that runs in user mode that has a switch statement for the different operation types and makes separate syscalls (that do not have variable argument lists) for each one. That will mitigate all the concerns I have.

@andrewboie 

> You've had two people, including the chair of the Zephyr Security Working Group explain to you that this shouldn't be done. 

Yeah, two people said that something shouldn't be done, I'm just not sure what they refer to. For example, @d3zd3z comment is attached to the function which is called **only from kernel-mode code**, so has nothing to do with syscalling from userspace to kernelspace.

Anyway, this is not ready for review yet, until it passed CI, so converted back to draft, and afterwards I'll be querying who means what in detail.

> For my part, my patience is completely exhausted.

Well, that means your inability/indesire to support your subsystem, and coach your colleagues by the project, even on the visibly complex/challenging tasks, which require your involvement - all that being sad.

> I'll review your patches again when it has some +1's from your colleagues from Linaro. Get some internal buy-in and come back.

This work is not related to my current task assignments in Linaro, it's based on my responsibilities as ~~maintainer~~ codeowner of the POSIX subsystem, triggered by accumulated technical debt of insufficient test coverage of some configuration options, all related to userspace/kernel split. So, you are still the best party to provide discussion and consultation on these matters.

@pfalcon passion for what we work on is a good thing but don't let it cross into a point of being a ****. 

As for using the variadic functions in C you have to be careful because many security based groups consider using it in C as a high security risk primarily because there is a lack of type checking. 

There is also a MISRA rule (Rule 17.1: https://gitlab.com/MISRA/MISRA-C/MISRA-C-2012/Example-Suite/-/blob/master/R_17_01.c) that you need to be careful of and ensure that the code doesn't run up against since we have adopted coding standards that will start being enforced on the kernel code.

It does appear that you have separated the variadic function interface from the syscall interface with the marshaling you did. That probably works if the syscall on the ioctl can verify the memory space of the array passed based on the n_args value passed in. I'm not sure though what additional validation is needed on the individual arguments in the array though?

> I'm not sure though what additional validation is needed on the individual arguments in the array though?

@dleach02  That's the problem: the individual arguments needs to be validated. They could contain pointer values, and if so every single one of them needs to be bounded and checked for appropriate access. We can't just unmarshal them on the kernel side and call it a day handing them off to the implementation; if the implementation treats any of the args as a pointer and not an integral value we have a potential exploit because none of these pointers have been validated.

What we have here is a variadic interface to send up to N arbitrary uintptr_t arguments to the kernel, with no knowledge on the kernel side what these arguments actually represent, since the verification is being done in a generic verifier for any ioctl.

This generic interface will not work, the particular semantics of the arguments entirely depend on what the particular function is. Which is why I asked to just demux ioctl calls in userspace and send them each as different syscalls.

Now that I think of it, there's also the problem that there's no accounting for what threads can use what file descriptors, unless I am missing something a malicious thread could manipulate any file descriptor active in the system in the current design. That's something that should probably be looked at separately.

> Now that I think of it, there's also the problem that there's no accounting for what threads can use what file descriptors, unless I am missing something a malicious thread could manipulate any file descriptor active in the system in the current design. That's something that should probably be looked at separately.

Yep. That's a biggie.

> Yep. That's a biggie.

Indeed, that's a "biggie":

File descriptors are per process, not per thread. So whoever will implement support for multiple processes in Zephyr, will also make sure that fdtable is per-process.

@andrewboie, I understand what you are saying. We should clarify (if it isn't already done), what the rules are for validating the parameters in a system call. It seems like the rule you are articulating is that all parameters must be properly typed and known at the time of the call and they must be able to be properly verified. Hiding the type of the parameter is not allowed.

I'm assuming the baseline problem is that the IOCTL is directed at different underlying drivers/interfaces and as such, the interpretation of the data is different depending on the driver needs. The generic interface of the IOCTL will not be able to be supported via a syscall. If the "syscall" happens lower where the user space code takes in the IOCTL and then breaks out the parameters of the veriadic that could potentially be a syscall point of entry that could validate the parameters?

> > Yep. That's a biggie.

> File descriptors are per process, not per thread. So whoever will implement support for multiple processes in Zephyr, will also make sure that fdtable is per-process.

Of course. I didn't want to go on a diatribe, but obviously processes, permissions, pre-opened file descriptors (stdin, stdout, stderr), virtual devfs, console on serial port, etc. However, currently Zephyr *does* attempt to separate thread permissions based on (physical / virtual) address space and metadata. So even though the entire "process" has a flat set of file descriptors, certain threads really shouldn't be able to write to some file descriptors and until processes are implemented, fd's may need to have permissions associated with a thread or thread group.
@cfriedt: Show me a reference to *the* general purpose POSIX standard which says that, and we'll discuss it (later).

> Yep. That's a biggie.

Permission accounting is a must-have in order to introduce these syscalls, you wouldn't want Minecraft to be able read Firefox's file descriptors at-will. I have a solution I'm testing to fix this for sockets (we used to have it but it broke, it uses kernel object permissions) that should be generalize-able

About ioctl(): consider for a moment that although having syscalls with arbitrary variadic argument types is a nightmare, nobody I know of against having an extensible vectored driver interface mechanism...there's no requirement to use ioctl()'s interface specifically, ioctls aren't portable anyway and you can always write wrappers

have a look at how Windows does it: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/ioapiset/nf-ioapiset-deviceiocontrol?redirectedfrom=MSDN their definition with a device, handle, and in/out buffers would be trivial to validate in a syscall

As far as `ioctl` calls go, maybe we can glean something from how this is implemented in various Unixy platforms. The 'request' value is not a general number, but various bits within the number have meaning. Two of the bits indicate the direction that the data parameter moves, and then a range of the value indicates the size of the data pointer. It effectively maps the command number directly to the size and direction of the payload. The only calls that have to do additional validation are those that have additional pointers in the block being checked.

issue_context.title: No tests/samples covering socket read()/write() calls
issue_context.body: While support for POSIX read()/write() calls was implemented for some time (enabled by CONFIG_POSIX_API option), there're no tests or samples using this feature. This can lead to regressions and must be addressed.
comments: Reopening, as there're more work to do (https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/25443).
I'll add a sample demonstrating read / write functionality. Thanks for the suggestion!

This ticket actually goes far beyond simple examples (and IIRC, we do have examples of `read()` / `write()` now).

It raises the larger question.

**Do POSIX calls need to be system calls or is POSIX just a library?**

There is no kernel object associated with the global file descriptor table, so right now it's use is "free".

Additionally, there are no system-call level checks (`Z_OOPS()`) for reading or writing outside of the permitted memory region for the current thread (`CONFIG_USERSPACE`).

That means, for systems *with* an MMU / MPU we'll just get a fault, but then for systems without an MMU / MPU, it will result in random corruption.

However, that reflects the same behaviour for libraries today.

I'm tempted to close this `-EWONTFIX`, but I know that may be a contentious topic, so I'll mark it for review in the Architecture meeting.

The Arch meeting was cancelled on the day this was supposed to be reviewed, so I'll just jot down some notes:

I've converted the socketpair example to use read / write as well. Will close this issue.

However, I think there are some valid concerns with Zephyr's `fdtable.c`, but at the same time, it's not clear if Zephyr is really the place to focus on this sort of thing.
* the global collection of file descriptors is, well.. global
* there is no separation between kernel, userspace, or even other threads in terms of file descriptor use
* indeed, there is no file descriptor kernel object (such that permissions would be granted, etc)

This relates back to how file descriptor tables operate on POSIX systems; each process has its own file descriptor table (they are just integers) that refer to kernel file descriptor objects, a specific set of file operations.

That's a pretty heavyweight design though.

Some might argue that Zephyr's view of running in a single address space / process space is fine for its intended purposes.

Going to close this as done for now, but we can always reopen the topic in an architecture meeting.

review_comments:
It's important here that the VA argument to ioctl can only ever be a single argument. Older specs took advantage of looser typing rules in C, and this is only really a way of allowing various pointer types to be passed to this function. It is quite reasonable to make this a single pointer argument.

It might also be helpful to look at the Linux implementation (or BSD), which uses various bits of the request to determine exactly how much data is expected in this argument, and even which direction data flows.

We definitely shouldn't be passing n_args/args through the systemcall. A single pointer is fine.

> It might also be helpful to look at the Linux implementation (or BSD)

I don't try to "lift" implementation from other systems, together with associated copyright and licensing issues. I'm definitely aware of Linux maintainers' dislike for ioctl(), and understand why - just as ioctl() was a nice, clean, clever idea in the original Unix, just as it is unnice and unclear with all the "modern systems".

> We definitely shouldn't be passing n_args/args through the systemcall. A single pointer is fine.

Someone will need to elaborate in detail on those points.

It's otherwise pretty clear that syscall validation rules will need to be extended for the ioctl() case. That's why I'm questioning @andrewboie for details on both (intended) design and (actual) implementation of them.

My point here is that that "..." in the ioctl call is a modern artifact, and that ioctl calls should always have exactly one pointer argument. The "..." is needed because it isn't really possible to get it right as some kind of generic pointer. But, there should never be an instance of 2, or more arguments.

@d3zd3z:

> My point here is that that "..." in the ioctl call is a modern artifact

Can you elaborate on this a bit more? ("modern artifact")

> But, there should never be an instance of 2, or more arguments.

Regardless of the possible answer to the above question, the reason why ioctl() was brought in here is to exactly allow passing multiple arguments. ioctl() is used both for userspace->kernel and kernel->kernel communication. userspace->kernel subset if really lean so far - as you may imagine, nobody wants to add the complete Linux mess in there. The usecase behind supporting userspace ioctl() is, well, application portability POSIX-ish systems -> Zephyr. I.e. as people will port more apps, they will find ioctl() request types needed, and can implement then, then maybe even contribute upstream (maybe keep out of tree in forks). The ideas is, again, to provide a general interface which would work for any request type (and its params).

Now, kernel->kernel ioctl is used to generically implement some processing between implementations of the same interface (file descriptor) in kernel. E.g., there's a generic implementation of poll(), which uses kernel-ioctl to implement processing sub-steps polymorphically across different file descriptor objects. And ioctl is used there to save on the code size. The more ironically that protected userspace now adds much more overhead to it (i.e. no-split: code size savings comparing to "middle line", split kernel/userspace - code size bloat).

You're looking exactly at the support APIs for kernel->kernel ioctls.

All this may be not ideal, but nothing is ideal here, I look at support infra/docs for syscalls, and find it not ideal. This patch has a specific goal - set framework to allow all this work with kernel/userspace split. It doesn't do any further revolutions, where varargs calls were used before for kernel-kernel ioctl, there they're used now.

> My point here is that that "..." in the ioctl call is a modern artifact, and that ioctl calls should always have exactly one pointer argument. The "..." is needed because it isn't really possible to get it right as some kind of generic pointer. But, there should never be an instance of 2, or more arguments.

@d3zd3z indeed, this is obvious from the documentation:

```
DESCRIPTION         top

       The ioctl() system call manipulates the underlying device parameters
       of special files.  In particular, many operating characteristics of
       character special files (e.g., terminals) may be controlled with
       ioctl() requests.  The argument fd must be an open file descriptor.

       The second argument is a device-dependent request code.  The third
       argument is an untyped pointer to memory.  It's traditionally char
       *argp (from the days before void * was valid C), and will be so named
       for this discussion.

       An ioctl() request has encoded in it whether the argument is an in
       parameter or out parameter, and the size of the argument argp in
       bytes.  Macros and defines used in specifying an ioctl() request are
       located in the file <sys/ioctl.h>.
```

ioctl() never been something you can send lots of arguments, and this is not ambiguous: 

> The third argument is an untyped pointer to memory.  It's traditionally char *argp (from the days before void * was valid C), and will be so named  for this discussion.

> The third argument is an untyped pointer to memory.

Ok, as explained above, ->ioctl() is used to implement both userspace->kernel (let's call it just "ioctl") and kernel->kernel (let's call it "kioctl") functions. While userspace ioctl() accepts only one param, it's a matter of fact that kioctl() accepts of multiple. I explained why this was done - to save on the size of vtable pointers and function prologues/epilogues. Good or bad, that's how it is. If someone wants to change that, go ahead and submit a proposal and prototype refactor.

This patch is concerned with different matter - allowing ioctl() to work across userspace/kernel, while preserving how it works currently for kernel->kernel. (I agree that if userspace # of arg is fixed, the patch can be simplified. If there's something to say, then it's that I shouldn't have started on that while being assigned to other big and deep tasks, and multitasking among them, forgetting and overlooking such points.)
